```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 100)
```

A classic use of constrained triangulation is to rebuild a surface from
contour lines. The contours are constraints, each vertex carries its height,
and the triangulation fills in between. This vignette does that for a 6 km
square around kunanyi (Mount Wellington) in Tasmania, then checks the surface
against the elevation model that the contours came from.

```{r setup}
library(cdtr)
```

## The data

The contours (every 50 m, simplified to 5 m) and a 40 m grid of the source
elevations are in a small file shipped with the package. The source is the
Tasmania 2 m digital elevation model, The LIST, (c) State of Tasmania, under a
Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia licence. The script that made the
file is in the package source as `data-raw/tas_wellington.R`.

```{r data}
d <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "tas_wellington.rds", package = "cdtr"))
contours <- d$contours
head(contours)
length(unique(contours$line))
```

Each row is a vertex of a contour line (`line` identifies the line) with
its height `z`. Coordinates are metres in GDA94 / MGA zone 55.

## Contours as a PSLG

The segments join each vertex to the next one on the same line.

```{r pslg}
n <- nrow(contours)
same_line <- contours$line[-n] == contours$line[-1]
s0 <- which(same_line)
s1 <- s0 + 1L
c(vertices = n, segments = length(s0))
```

The contours are only constraints; there is no boundary ring, so the mesh
covers the convex hull of the contour vertices (`erase = "hull"`). Where an
input has no boundary there is nothing for `"outer"` to erase against.

`cdt_triangulate_attr()` carries `z` along and gives any new vertex a height
interpolated from the constrained triangulation of the input.

```{r mesh}
m <- cdt_triangulate_attr(contours$x, contours$y, s0, s1,
                          PA = cbind(z = contours$z), erase = "hull")
c(vertices = nrow(m$P), triangles = nrow(m$T), crossings = m$n_crossing)
```

```{r plot-mesh}
plot_surface <- function(m, main = "") {
  zt <- rowMeans(matrix(m$PA[t(m$T), "z"], ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))
  pal <- hcl.colors(100, "Terrain 2")
  col <- pal[cut(zt, 100, labels = FALSE)]
  plot(m$P, type = "n", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main)
  polygon(m$P[t(cbind(m$T, NA)), 1], m$P[t(cbind(m$T, NA)), 2],
          col = col, border = NA)
}
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0))
plot_surface(m, "triangles shaded by mean height")
par(op)
```

## How good is the surface?

The source elevations are at 40 m cell centres. Interpolating the mesh to those
points with `cdt_interpolate()` gives a check that does not depend on
how the contours were drawn. `cdt_locate()` says which points fall outside
the hull of the contours, where there is no surface to compare.

```{r grid}
g <- d$grid
nr <- nrow(g$z); nc <- ncol(g$z)
cell <- 40
xq <- rep(g$xmin + (seq_len(nc) - 0.5) * cell, each = nr)
yq <- rep(g$ymax - (seq_len(nr) - 0.5) * cell, times = nc)
zq <- as.vector(g$z)

inside <- !is.na(cdt_locate(m$P, m$T, xq, yq))
mean(inside)

surface_error <- function(m) {
  zz <- cdt_interpolate(m$P, m$T, m$PA, xq[inside], yq[inside])[, "z"]
  err <- zz - zq[inside]
  c(rmse = sqrt(mean(err^2)), mean_error = mean(err), max_abs = max(abs(err)))
}
round(surface_error(m), 2)
```

The root mean square error is about 7 m, with contours 50 m apart, and the
average error is close to zero. The largest errors, tens of metres, are where
the ground changes height between widely spaced lines: a linear mesh cannot
put a peak above its highest contour or a hollow below its lowest, since it has
no vertices there.

## Quality

Triangles built only from contour vertices can be long and thin, since all
the vertices lie on the lines. `cdt_quality()` reports it.

```{r quality}
summary(cdt_quality(m)[c("min_angle", "radius_edge")])
```

Adding Steiner vertices by refinement improves the shape of the triangles.
Does it improve the surface? Refine to a maximum area and a minimum angle, and
compare the same measures.

```{r refine}
mr <- cdt_triangulate_attr(contours$x, contours$y, s0, s1,
                           PA = cbind(z = contours$z), erase = "hull",
                           max_area = 2000, min_angle = 25)
qa <- cdt_quality(m)
qb <- cdt_quality(mr)
rbind(
  contours_only = c(triangles = nrow(m$T), median_min_angle = median(qa$min_angle),
                    share_below_20 = mean(qa$min_angle < 20), surface_error(m)["rmse"]),
  refined = c(triangles = nrow(mr$T), median_min_angle = median(qb$min_angle),
              share_below_20 = mean(qb$min_angle < 20), surface_error(mr)["rmse"])
) |> round(3)
```

Refinement makes the triangles much better shaped (far fewer with a minimum
angle below 20 degrees), at the cost of five times as many triangles, but the
surface error is essentially unchanged. The new vertices only carry heights that
the contours already imply. The extra triangles are for anything that
needs well-shaped elements, such as rendering or a finite element model, and
not for accuracy. For a better surface there must be more information, such as
spot heights along ridges and streams, which can be added as vertices with their
own `z`.

```{r plot-refined}
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0))
plot_surface(mr, "refined: area and minimum angle")
par(op)
```

The `unrefined` component of the result says where refinement could not meet
its targets, and a few triangles remain well below the 25 degree target.

```{r unrefined}
mr$unrefined[, c("criterion", "circumcenterOutside", "shortEdgeTriangles",
                 "sharpFixedCorner")]
qr <- cdt_quality(mr)
sum(qr$min_angle < 5)
```

Those few triangles are mostly right at the edge of the mesh. The convex hull is
not itself a constraint here, so its edge is not something the refiner can split
to improve the triangles beside it. If a clean outer edge matters, add a
bounding polygon to the constraints.
